## ARGUMENT

**I. Article 35's two-year period is not an absolute jurisdictional bar, and equitable considerations may excuse a late filing.**

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the "right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air art. 35(1), May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45. The defendant treats "extinguished" as the end of the inquiry. But a condition precedent to suit is not the same as a jurisdictional limit, and the Convention itself leaves room for domestic law. Article 35(2) provides that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seized of the case." *Id.* art. 35(2). That text directs the Court to the forum's rules for computing the period, and those rules include the settled federal doctrines of tolling and suspension.

Treaty interpretation begins with the text and its ordinary meaning, and a court should not read into a treaty a rigidity its drafters did not write. Nothing in Article 35 says that forum tolling principles are displaced. The Supreme Court presumes that nonjurisdictional filing deadlines are subject to equitable tolling unless Congress or the text clearly says otherwise. *Irwin v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs*, 498 U.S. 89, 95–96 (1990); *Holland v. Florida*, 560 U.S. 631, 645–49 (2010). Characterizing a deadline as a "condition precedent" does not change that presumption. It describes what the plaintiff must plead and prove, not whether the forum's tolling rules apply.

The Eleventh Circuit applies equitable tolling where a litigant shows diligence and extraordinary circumstances beyond the litigant's control. *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271–72 (11th Cir. 1999) (tolling is appropriate when a limitations period is missed through circumstances that are "both beyond [the litigant's] control and unavoidable even with diligence"); *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261–62 (11th Cir. 2006) (applying equitable tolling to a statutory period and describing the doctrine's two requirements); *Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1478–79 (11th Cir. 1993) (applying equitable tolling to a statutory limitations period for suits against the United States). The court has also recognized that the doctrine is reserved for extraordinary circumstances, *Bost v. Fed. Express Corp.*, 372 F.3d 1233, 1242 (11th Cir. 2004), and Plaintiff accepts that burden. As set out in the record, Plaintiff pursued her claim diligently, and the late filing resulted from [describe the extraordinary circumstance, with record citations]. These facts, not any lapse by Plaintiff, caused the delay. Whether they meet the standard is a fact-bound question that the district court should not have resolved against Plaintiff as a matter of law.

**II. Alternatively, the carrier's bankruptcy tolled or suspended the period.**

Even if Article 35 admits no equitable tolling, the carrier's bankruptcy independently suspended the period. The filing of a bankruptcy petition operates as an automatic stay of "the commencement or continuation" of any judicial action against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the petition. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). The stay is broad. Actions taken in violation of it are generally void, and the stay's reach is measured by the claim asserted against the debtor. *Jove Eng'g, Inc. v. IRS*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546–55 (11th Cir. 1996) (describing the stay's scope and the consequences of acts that violate it). A plaintiff who is barred from suing the debtor cannot be charged with failing to "bring" an action against it during the stay.

The Bankruptcy Code also addresses this situation directly. Where a nonbankruptcy period for commencing an action against a debtor has not expired before the petition date, section 108(c) extends the period until the later of the original deadline or thirty days after notice of termination of the stay. 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). Article 35(2) incorporates the "law of the court seized" for calculating the period. Because the forum's law includes the Bankruptcy Code, section 108(c) is part of how the period is computed here. Applying it respects the Convention's text. It does not rewrite the treaty. Because Plaintiff filed within the extended period, the action was timely.

**III. Conclusion.**

The Court should reverse the dismissal, hold that Article 35 does not foreclose equitable tolling or the operation of the bankruptcy stay and section 108(c), and remand for the district court to apply those doctrines to the record.
